$description: Grammar Hub — canonical grammar model (taxonomy). One shared source of MEANING for how the apps identify grammatical categories. It does NOT unify the analysis engines (Desgramatizador = compromise.js NLP, Question Lab = hand-written rules / vanilla no-deps, Grammaster = generation). It defines the categories and their relationships, which each app maps onto at its own granularity, so the same word is understood the same way across apps. `colorRole` values reference the role keys in Apps/design-tokens (tokens.json).

pos.description: Word class / part of speech. Finest granularity. Used by Desgramatizador POS mode.

auxiliary.label: AUX
auxiliary.name: Auxiliary
auxiliary.def: helper verb (be / have / do) supporting a main verb

modal.label: MOD
modal.name: Modal
modal.def: can, could, will, should, must… — modality

adverb.label: ADV
adverb.name: Adverb
adverb.def: modifies a verb, adjective or adverb

structure.description: Functional role in the clause — which slot a word or phrase fills. Coarser than POS. Used by Desgramatizador structure mode and Grammaster's sentence colouring.

S.name: Subject
S.def: who or what does the action

AUX.name: Auxiliary
AUX.def: helper in the verb phrase (includes modals, functionally)

A.name: Adverbial
A.def: when? / where? / how? (also verb-region adverbs: ever, never, always…)

question.description: Pieces of a question and its answer. Question Lab's model.

wh-word.name: Wh-word
wh-word.def: what is asked; never bounces into the answer

auxiliary.name: Auxiliary
auxiliary.def: carries the tense (do/does/did, be, have, will, modals)

semi-aux.name: Semi-aux
semi-aux.def: going to / used to / have to — auxiliary unit; the 'to' belongs here and the main verb follows in base form

subject.name: Subject
subject.def: who / what; bounces into the answer (you → I)

adverb.name: Adverb
adverb.def: ever, never, always, often… — modifies the verb; its own piece

new-info.name: New info
new-info.def: what you add when answering; not from the question

relationships.rule: Main verb + auxiliary + semi-aux form one 'verb system', shown in the same colour family (the reds). Verb carries the heavier/darker red, auxiliary the lighter rose.
A modal is its own word class in POS (MOD), but functionally it fills the auxiliary slot. The structure and question layers show it as AUX. Teach it as 'modals are structural auxiliaries'.
be / have / do are auxiliaries ONLY when a main verb follows. Alone (copular 'be', possessive 'have') they ARE the main verb (V), not an auxiliary.

'going to', 'used to', 'have to' are auxiliary UNITS: the 'to' belongs to the (semi-)auxiliary, and the main verb that follows is in base form. Shown as AUX (auxiliary family) everywhere — Desgramatizador (POS + structure), Grammaster, and Question Lab (which labels them 'semi-aux'). A modal is likewise a functional subtype of auxiliary.
When the wh-word IS the subject (e.g. 'Who painted the Mona Lisa?') there is no auxiliary and the verb is conjugated.
The negator 'not' / 'n't' stays with the auxiliary (parallel to the fused 'doesn't'), but it is a negative ADVERB — apps may signal that (Desgramatizador tints the 'not' amber inside the AUX block).

Verb-region adverbs (ever, never, always, often, just…) are their own adverb category, shown at EVERY level — Desgramatizador puts them in A (adverbial); Question Lab shows them as an 'adverb' piece. Never dropped, never merged into the verb. Deliberate leveling: at Básico/Elemental only these single-word frequency adverbs get A; broader adverbial PHRASES (yesterday, at home) stay in C until Intermedio, where the O/A distinction is introduced.

questionLab.granularity: question pieces only; the analyzer is universal, curated content gated by CEFR

grammaster.granularity: coarse subject / auxiliary / verb / complement colouring of the sentence it builds
